rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic ordering follows context; the text may place a lesser thing before a superior one or a later thing before an earlier one.
rows.anchor: التقديم والتأخير في القرآن عموماً مرتبط بسياق الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-Layl, the afterlife comes first because its seeker was mentioned first; this world is delayed to match the one who seeks it.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى قدم الآخرة لتقدم طالبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qasas places this world first because its surrounding passage recalls worldly blessings and calls for gratitude; mentioning praise and thanks suits that context.
rows.anchor: السياق كله في الدنيا وما أودع الله تعالى من النعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Layl omits praise, foregrounds God’s ownership of both realms, and therefore begins with the afterlife, as explained above.
rows.anchor: لم يذكر الحمد وقدم الآخرة كما سبق وفصلنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word al-dunyā derives from أدنى and can mean nearer, lower, lesser, or inferior; those senses do not suit a passage stressing God’s vast dominion.
rows.anchor: الدنيا نفسها هي مؤنث الأدنى ومن معانيها الأقرب والأخس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is guidance promised in 92:12 and concerns the afterlife, linking the fire warning to God’s ownership of both realms.
rows.anchor: أنذرنا هو من الهدى الذي ينبه الله تعالى منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Layl mentions warning without glad tidings, so it names the Fire alone; Paradise would be a promise of good outside this warning passage’s purpose.
rows.anchor: ذكر الله تعالى الإنذار ولم يذكر التبشير ولذلك اقتصر على ذكر النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wretched person’s denial covers all faith, while turning away means abandoning obedience and engaging in sins.
rows.anchor: بمعنى كذب بكل مفردات الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Denial answers belief in the good, and turning away answers giving and piety; withholding is itself a form of turning away.
rows.anchor: كذب مقابل (وصدق بالحسنى) وتولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses reaffirm and broaden the earlier description: turning away exceeds miserliness and self-sufficiency, and denial exceeds denial of the good.
rows.anchor: التولي أعم من البخل والاستغناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because this denial and turning away are more general, their consequence is worse: blazing Fire for the wretched, compared with the earlier easier outcome.
rows.anchor: لما عمّ السوء وانتشر أصبحت العاقبة أشد من الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past tense frames a single, completed warning of one thing, the blazing Fire; warnings tied to ongoing revelation use the present tense.
rows.anchor: جاء الفعل بصيغة المضارع لأن الله تعالى أنذرهم هنا بشيء واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Naba’s warning is emphatic because its warning is extended and repeated throughout the sūra; al-Layl gives one warning in one verse and needs no added emphasis.
rows.anchor: سورة النبأ فيها توكيد لأن الإنذار في سورة النبأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying only the most pious will avoid the Fire would wrongly imply that other believers cannot be spared; God’s wording instead leaves His mercy open to them too.
rows.anchor: وهذا من رحمة الله تعالى بعباده لأن معنى الآية أن الله تعالى يجنب الأتقى وغير الأتقى أيضاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Fire is restricted to the wretched, but the act of sparing is unrestricted, expressing that God’s mercy precedes His wrath.
rows.anchor: في العذاب حصر (لا يصلاها إلا الأشقى الذي كذب وتولى) وفي الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opposite of the wretched is described at the highest level: the most pious gives his own wealth to purify himself, an image of maximal giving and sincerity.
rows.anchor: الأتقى الذي يؤتي ماله يتزكى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier passage moves from particular acts toward a general description of evil; the good passage rises from giving to the highest piety and purification.
rows.anchor: وفي الحسنة ترقى من الأفضل إلى الأفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive verb signals that the pious person is spared by God, the creator of people and Fire, rather than escaping through his own power.
rows.anchor: الله تعالى هو الذي يجنب عباده النار ولا أحد يستطيع أن يتجنبها بنفسه أبداً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People cannot save themselves from the Fire, even when they are the most pious and give their wealth in purification.
rows.anchor: لا يستطيع الناس أن ينجوا بأنفسهم من النار ولو كان أحدهم الأتقى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deliverance may follow entry into harm and suffering, whereas sparing means being kept away before the harm is reached; the most pious is spared altogether.
rows.anchor: التنجية قد تكون بعد الوقوع في الشيء ومعاناته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses deliverance with those who are pious and sparing with the singular superlative, since the latter is kept from the trial itself.
rows.anchor: مع اتقوا يستعمل القرآن لفظ (التنجية) ومع الأتقى يستعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The giver owes nobody repayment for a favor; he gives solely for God’s face, without expectation of a return, which is the fullest sincerity.
rows.anchor: ليس لأحد فضل فيجازيه عليه وإنما يفعله خالصاً لوجه الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If hill means a person whose sanctity may be violated, the verse depicts the Prophet under hardship as his people fight and try to kill him.
rows.anchor: بمعنى (مستحل) لا تراعى حرمته فهو دليل على أنه في كبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If hill means lawful in the sanctuary, the Prophet is permitted to kill and capture; this reading places the unbelievers in hardship and Muslims in strength.
rows.anchor: وهو (حلال في البلد) أي ضد الحرام فهو - صلى الله عليه وسلم - يحلّ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath’s mention of parent and child links childbirth and child-rearing, both requiring hardship and persistence, to the obstacle and its hungry day.
rows.anchor: الولادة مشقة وعنت وتحتاج إلى مثابرة وقوة للتربية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the Qur’an’s only use of ‘destroyed’ for money; the word fits the sūra’s hardship, death, obstacle, famine, and wasteful spending, where money spent wrongly is ruined.
rows.anchor: هذه هي الآية الوحيدة في القرآن كله التي استعمل فيها الإهلاك مع المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lubad means much gathered together and may be an intensive singular or a plural of lubda; the gathered mass suits the hostile crowds assembled against the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وفيها احتمالان: قد تكون مفرد صيغة مبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of gathering recurs across the sūra, and ‘much’ alone would miss this shared sense; the wording serves the sūra’s rhetoric.
rows.anchor: الكثرة لا تنفي الاجتماع لذلك اختيار الإهلاك واللبد متناسب جداً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing is more specific than knowing: the speaker imagines no one watched his spending, while God observes details and knows all creatures’ acts.
rows.anchor: الرؤية أهمّ وأخصّ من العلم وهناك فرق بين العلم بالشيء ورؤيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past ‘did not see him’ concerns his alleged past spending, while the future-oriented ‘will not be able’ follows his gaining strength and confidence in his defenses.
rows.anchor: أيحسب أن لم يره أحد أنه أنفق المال في أمور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two eyes answer the claim that no one saw him; the tongue and lips answer his boast about spending, making God’s gifts evidence of His knowledge and power.
rows.anchor: جاءت كلمة عينين وهما أداة الرؤية مقابل قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Najd is the Qur’an’s distinctive word for a raised, difficult path; unlike the easy, well-traveled sabīl, it matches the sūra’s hardship and struggle.
rows.anchor: النجد يعني الطريق المرتفع

rows.speaker: أغلب المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators understand the two elevated paths as the path of good and the path of evil.
rows.anchor: وأغلب المفسرين قالوا أنه يعني طريق الخير وطريق الشر

rows.speaker: الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says one should not favor the path of evil over the path of good; the author calls this the closer interpretation.
rows.anchor: وعن الرسول - صلى الله عليه وسلم - (لا يكن نجد الشرّ أحبّ إليكم من نجد الخير)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance to the two paths means showing them, not guaranteeing a good destination: the road can lead to the Fire.
rows.anchor: فهي تكون بمعنى الدلالة على الطريقين طريق الخير وطريق الشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary Arabic, lā does not negate the past unless repeated; otherwise past negation normally uses mā, so the verse’s construction needs explanation.
rows.anchor: لا تنفي الفعل الماضي إلا إذا كررت

rows.speaker: قسم من المفسرين
rows.claim: Some commentators treat lā as negation and cite Arab poetry, although the author says the example is outside normal Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: قسم من المفسرين قال قد تفيد النفي واستشهدوا على ذلك ببعض ما ورد في أشعار العرب

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some read lā as a prayer against the person who wasted his wealth, asking that he not scale the obstacle until he reforms.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال إنها تفيد الدعاء وليس النفي

rows.speaker: قسم آخر
rows.claim: Another group reads lā as future negation, permitted when a past-form verb has future meaning, as in the cited oath-like example.
rows.anchor: وقسم آخر رأوا أنها تفيد نفي الإستقبال

rows.speaker: ومنهم
rows.claim: Some understand an elided interrogative hamza, making the phrase a rebuke for failing to scale the obstacle and an exhortation to do so.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال إنها استفهام وقد حذفت همزة الإستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle gathers negation, prayer, future negation, and interrogation together: it condemns past failure, warns of future failure, and urges reform; another particle could not carry all these readings.
rows.anchor: قد جمعت كل هذه المعاني التي ذكرنا وفيها احتمالات النفي والدعاء والإستقبال والإستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating al-ʿaqaba magnifies and makes its trial imposing; Qur’anic parallels include the repeated names al-Qāriʿa and al-Ḥāqqa.
rows.anchor: جاء التكرار للتفخيم والتهويل والتعظيم لأمر العقبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Across the Qur’an, mā adrāka in the past is followed by an explanation, while mā yudrīka in the present leaves the matter unanswered and vague.
rows.anchor: وإذا استعمل (أدراك) بصيغة الماضي يتبعها بالتفصيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated explicit noun is stronger than a pronoun; the more intense obstacle context favors repeating al-ʿaqaba rather than using ‘it’ as in al-Qāriʿa.
rows.anchor: الإسم الظاهر أقوى من الكناية أو الضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Humaza expands both the sinners’ traits and their torment, describing God’s Fire and its enclosure; that more elaborate context likewise repeats al-ḥuṭama.
rows.anchor: هنا جاء بـ (نار الله) وفي القارعة (نار) فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using aw gives alternatives suited to a person’s ability; with waw, freeing a captive and feeding both needy groups would all be required, contrary to the author’s reading of God’s mercy.
rows.anchor: وهذا من باب التخيير فالإنسان يختار ما يستطيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yatīman is the direct object of the verbal noun iṭʿām.
rows.anchor: يتيماً مفعول به للمصدر إطعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some exegetes distinguish the poor person, unable to meet daily needs, from the needy person, who has work or income but still lacks enough; the boat workers in al-Kahf are evidence.
rows.anchor: المفسرون بين الفقير والمسكين وقالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A miskīn with matraba is exceptionally poor, as if stuck to the dirt, with no shelter and lying on the roadside.
rows.anchor: هو المسكين الفقير الذي لا مأوى له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Freeing a captive comes first because Islam values liberation; a debtor or wanted person may be unable to seek food and may be in greater need than an orphan or poor person.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى عِظم الحرية في الإسلام إذا كان بمعنى الرِّق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orphan follows because a child below puberty cannot fend for himself on a famine day; the older needy person may be able to seek food.
rows.anchor: هذا الصغير اليتيم في مثل هذا اليوم ينبغي أن يُراعى ويُتفقد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order also moves from fewer to more people: debtors or captives are rare, orphans more numerous, and the poor most numerous; orphanhood ends at maturity.
rows.anchor: فهي مرتبة بحسب الحاجة في ذلك الوقت وهي مرتبة بحسب القلّة والكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-maymana can mean the right-hand side, people given their records in the right hand, or the blessed; their good benefits themselves and others.
rows.anchor: الميمنة لها ثلاثة دلالات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mashʾama can mean the left side, people given records in the left, or those bringing ill fortune on themselves and others by refusing good and violating sanctity.
rows.anchor: والمشئمة أيضاً تحتمل ثلاثة دلالات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-maymana is broader than aṣḥāb al-yamīn because it includes blessing others through freeing and feeding, so the broader term suits the context.
rows.anchor: أصحاب الميمنة تختلف عن أصحاب اليمين لأنها أعمّ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit pronoun ‘they’ before the people of the left restricts that group to the disbelievers; it is not used for the people of the right, who are not limited to the earlier traits.
rows.anchor: أما الذين كفروا هو أصحاب المشئمة حصراً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muṣada means sealed shut, without light, exit, or relief; fronting ‘upon them’ restricts the sealed Fire to the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: تقديم الجار والمجرور هو للقصر بمعنى أنها مؤصدة عليهم حصراً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both muʾṣada and mūṣada are sound transmitted readings and are Arabic variants; readers may choose either rather than rank them as invalid.
rows.anchor: كلتا القراءتين متواترتين وكلتاهما من القراءات السبع الصحيحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author personally prefers the hamza form muʾṣada because its heavy sound suits the weight and hardship of the sūra.
rows.anchor: أختار لفظ (مؤصدة) بالهمزة لأنها مناسبة للحالة التي هم عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Humaza elaborates both the sinners’ qualities and their punishment, while al-Balad simply calls them disbelievers, explaining why the former details the Fire further.
rows.anchor: في سورة الهمزة نلاحظ أنه تعالى قد توسّع في ذكر صفات المعذّب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nominative wayl forms a nominal sentence and implies established, lasting ruin, matching the unopenable sealed Fire; accusative waylan is a verbal noun meaning that God imposes ruin.
rows.anchor: بالرفع في أول السورة تدل على الهلاك التام الدائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wayl is among source nouns whose verbs have fallen out of use; waylan is parsed as an accusative absolute, conventionally glossed ‘He destroyed him utterly.’
rows.anchor: كما أن ويل: هو مصدر من المصادر التي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Neither form is inherently stronger: eloquence selects the nominal or verbal sentence according to what the context requires.
rows.anchor: البلاغة في القرآن الكريم هو مطابقة الكلام لمقتضى الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afterlife is set against what came before: what lies ahead for the Prophet is better than his past, and the prefixed lām emphasizes this promise.
rows.anchor: ما يأتي خير لك أيها الرسول مما مضى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying ‘than the world’ would limit the promise to the afterlife and deny that the Prophet’s remaining life would bring better things; the verse also confirms the preceding reassurance.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية توكيد لما سبقها في قوله تعالى ما ودعك ربك وما قلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase specifies ‘for you’ because this sūra and al-Sharḥ address the Prophet; making the promise universal would fail for some people whose afterlife is worse than their worldly life.
rows.anchor: قال تعالى (وللآخرة خير لك من الأولى)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawfa marks the future, like the preceding promise, and the lām in wa-lasawfa repeats its emphasis.
rows.anchor: وجاء أيضاً باللام في (ولسوف) وأكده بنفس التوكيد باللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God leaves both gift and contentment unrestricted, names Himself as the Lord, and addresses the Prophet personally; each choice magnifies the honor and scope of the gift.
rows.anchor: أطلق سبحانه العطاء ولم يحدده إنما شمل هذا العطاء كل شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Contentment is among life’s greatest blessings: it brings peace and stability, while lack of it makes wealth, comfort, or ease feel like hardship and deprivation.
rows.anchor: الرضى هو من أجل النعم على الإنسان وهو أساس الاستقرار والطمأنينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra moves from darkness to light—orphanship to shelter, lostness to guidance, and need to wealth—in keeping with the claim that what comes later is better.
rows.anchor: بدأ سبحانه وتعالى بالظلمة ثم النور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation’s light is represented by forenoon; the quiet night followed the revelation, so the order of the oath reflects the later interruption of revelation.
rows.anchor: انقطاع الوحي هو الذي تأخر وليس العكس لذا جاء قسم الضحى أولاً ثم الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated ‘your Lord’ fits the orphan needing care, the lost needing guidance, and the needy needing provision; the Qur’an often links guidance with the Lord.
rows.anchor: الرب معناه انه هو المعلم والمربي والمرشد والقيم

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some commentators say the omitted object is obvious from context; others say omission preserves the verse endings.
rows.anchor: قسم قال إنها مراعاة لفواصل الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects rhyme as the controlling explanation: Qur’anic meaning comes first, as the cited Ṭā Hā example shows.
rows.anchor: القرآن الكريم لا يراعي الفاصلة على حساب المعنى مطلقاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omissions convey open-ended generosity: God sheltered, enriched, and guided the Prophet, through him, and for his sake many others as well.
rows.anchor: الحذف هنا جاء للإطلاق والدلالة على سعة الكرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s sheltering extended to many orphans; the author invokes the report that the caretaker of an orphan will be beside the Prophet in Paradise.
rows.anchor: أنا وكافل اليتيم كهاتين وأشار إلى إصبعيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God guided the Prophet and guided many people through him, as expressed by the verse that he guides to a straight path.
rows.anchor: وإنك لتهدي إلى صراط مستقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unrestricted sense of the omissions accords with the broad gift promised in 93:5; contextual clarity, rhyme, and broad meaning can all apply together.
rows.anchor: تناسب سعة الإطلاق هنا قوله تعالى (ولسوف يعطيك ربك فترضى)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence follows life’s order: orphanhood ends at puberty, then guidance is needed for moral responsibility and earning before one’s later state of poverty or wealth.
rows.anchor: هذا هو الترتيب الطبيعي في الحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qahr means harmful domination, including denying an orphan’s rights, oppressing or belittling him, and taking his property.
rows.anchor: القهر في اللغة: هو التسلط بما يؤذي

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Exegetes differ whether the asker is asking for money or charity, for knowledge and religious instruction, or whether the word covers both kinds.
rows.anchor: السائل اختلف المفسرون فيها فقال بعضهم: هو سائل المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whichever kind of asker is meant, one should not rebuke him: answer the poor kindly or respond to the seeker of religious knowledge.
rows.anchor: سواء كان السائل سائل مال وصدقة أو سائل علم ومعرفة يجب أن لا ينهر

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some commentators take the blessing as prophethood and its teachings; others take it as all good in this life or the next, or specifically the blessing of religion.
rows.anchor: أما النعمة فقال بعض المفسرين إنها النبوة وتعاليمها وقال آخرون إنها كل ما أصاب الإنسان من خير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author includes all these senses: one should proclaim the blessing of religion and speak of God’s worldly blessings, whose effects God loves to see.
rows.anchor: الواقع أن النعمة هنا أيضاً تشمل كل هذه المعاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taḥdīth entails repeating and spreading a message; mere informing can happen once, so the wording commands persistent, repeated proclamation.
rows.anchor: التحديث فهو يقتضي التكرار والإشاعة أكثر من مرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated ‘ḥaddathanā’ in hadith transmission illustrates how a report is passed on many times until it spreads.
rows.anchor: يكررون ذلك مرة أو مرات عديدة حتى يصلوا إلى أخبرنا رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orphan command directly follows the earlier mention of God sheltering the Prophet as an orphan.
rows.anchor: أما اليتيم فلا تقهر جاءت بنفس تسلسل الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The asker command fits both earlier blessings: an asker of money relates to God enriching the Prophet, and a seeker of knowledge relates to His guidance.
rows.anchor: السائل يشمل سائل العلم والمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speaking of worldly blessings comes last because the blessings must first occur; the preceding verses recount God’s favors on the Prophet.
rows.anchor: لا يمكن أن نتحدث عن النعمة إلا بعد وقوعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the blessing means religion, the preacher should first show good character, not oppress an orphan or rebuke a petitioner, before proclaiming it.
rows.anchor: على الداعية أن يتحلى بالخلق الكريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn suits the preceding discussion of revealed messages and joins religion with recompense; using a word for punishment alone would lose the religious sense.
rows.anchor: اختار كلمة (الدين) ولم يختر كلمة الجزاء أو الحساب أو النشور

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: One reported reading takes aḥkam al-ḥākimīn to mean the greatest in wisdom and best in governance; that wisdom entails resurrection and reward for good and bad deeds.
rows.anchor: أعظم ذوي الحكمة وأحسنهم تدبيراً

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Another reported reading understands the phrase as the most decisive judge, who judges between people in their disputes.
rows.anchor: أقضى القاضين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the wisdom reading, leaving people without accountability would contradict God’s wisdom, since it would fail to reward the good and punish the wrongdoer.
rows.anchor: حكمته تأبى أن يترك الإنسان سدى ولا يحاسب على أعماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine wisdom requires resurrection and recompense; settling disputes and rewarding people requires a judge, indeed the greatest judge.
rows.anchor: حكمته تقتضي الإعادة والجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥkam al-ḥākimīn can combine four senses: wisest rulers, most judicial of the wise, most judicial of judges, and wisest judges; aqḍā al-qāḍīn would convey only one.
rows.anchor: فيكون قد جمع أربعة معان كلها مرادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The confirmatory question invites the hearer to reach and voice the judgment, unlike a plain declarative statement.
rows.anchor: قرر المخاطب ليقوله بنفسه وليشترك في إصدار الحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra’s ending coheres with its opening: the one who sent the great revealed laws is the wisest of judges.
rows.anchor: فاتحة السورة في ذكر مواطن الرسالات العظمى وارتباطها بخاتمتها واضح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing words gather paired meanings: al-amīn suggests security and trustworthiness, asfal sāfilīn carries more than one sense, dīn joins religion and recompense, and aḥkam joins wisdom and judgment.
rows.anchor: فاختيرت (الأمين) لتجمع معنيي الأمن والأمانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kawthar answers al-Māʿūn point by point: abundant gift versus deprivation, prayer and sacrifice versus neglectful prayer and withholding food, and Paradise’s river versus denial of recompense.
rows.anchor: سورة الكوثر تأتي بعد سورة الماعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hater is truly cut off from good, as shown by the traits in al-Māʿūn: denial of judgment, neglect of orphans, failure to feed the poor, and heedless, ostentatious prayer.
rows.anchor: كل الصفات في هذه السورة تدل على الأبتر لأنه انقطع الخير عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kawthar fulfills the gift promised in al-Ḍuḥā; both the promise and fulfillment are emphasized, and prayer responds to the Lord who kept His promise.
rows.anchor: وسورة الكوثر هي انجاز لما وعد الله تعالى رسوله في سورة الضحى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting inna gives emphasis and focus: God alone gave this gift to His Prophet, and no one can remove what God bestowed.
rows.anchor: أهم أغراض التقديم هو الاهتمام والاختصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction marks both exclusive bestowal and special attention; what God alone gives His Prophet cannot be taken away by anyone.
rows.anchor: الله تعالى أعطى نبيه الكوثر اختصاصاً له وليس لأحد سواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inna is an emphatic pronoun of majesty.
rows.anchor: إنا: ضمير التعظيم ومؤكد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ātā is broader than aʿṭā, extending beyond material gifts to wisdom, signs, dominion, wealth, discernment, and revelation; aʿṭā generally concerns material things.
rows.anchor: آتى تستعمل لما هو أوسع من أعطى في اللغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The broader verb can include wisdom and discernment, for which aʿṭā is unsuitable; aʿṭā instead tends toward specific material bestowal.
rows.anchor: أما أعطى فهي تستعمل في الأمور المادية فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ītāʾ need not transfer ownership and can be revoked, while giving entails ownership and freedom to dispose of the gift; hence al-Kawthar is given as aʿṭā.
rows.anchor: الإيتاء ليس بالضرورة تمليكا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A revealed sign may be given to a prophet for delivery rather than private disposal; al-Kawthar, however, is given to the Prophet as his own to use freely.
rows.anchor: رب العالمين ملك رسوله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - الكوثر وأعطاه إياه تمليكاً له أن يتصرف فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kawthar’s intensive form conveys abundant good; unlike kathīr, it can denote the blessed thing itself, such as the river, as well as its exceptional goodness.
rows.anchor: الكوثر يدل على الكثرة المفرطة في الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kawthar covers the river, pool, renown, and every good given to the Prophet; it is abundance especially in goodness, whereas kathīr can be abundance of anything.
rows.anchor: كل ما قيل يشمل الخير الذي أعطاه الله تعالى لرسوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wāw in kawthar is stronger than yāʾ in a reported variant, so the wording chooses the stronger form for the greater gift.
rows.anchor: والواو أقوى من الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Omitting a qualifier such as water or wealth makes the gift unrestricted; the definite al- also encompasses the known river, while bare kawthar would not.
rows.anchor: حذف الموصوف أفاد الإطلاق وجمع كل الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unrestricted and immense gift suits the emphatic inna and majestic plural pronoun.
rows.anchor: يتناسب مع الخير الكثير والمطلق وناسبه التوكيد أيضاً في إنا
